findings.matters: Unassured company accounts and late submissions indicate either weak governance of group entities or emerging financial issues that the council does not yet fully understand.

Due to the final submission of the Business Plans from company boards only providing a few days to review, it has not been possible to provide full assurance of the Business Plans.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 resulted in a £14m reduction in 2026/27 funding compared to the sector's expectations after summer 2025 consultation, with financial impact 'increasing significantly' in subsequent years.
findings.detail: The government consulted on a reformed funding formula in June 2025 that, the council states, 'would have addressed the Council's repeated calls for fairer funding.' Post-consultation, 'the proposed formula was changed again to the significant detriment of the Council.' This resulted in a £14m reduction for 2026/27 alone, with the council noting the 'financial impact increasing significantly in subsequent years.' This is a structural funding change, not temporary.
findings.matters: A £14m cut plus larger cuts in subsequent years is a material revenue change outside the council's control, reducing its financial flexibility and increasing reliance on savings or reserves.
findings.figures: £14m reduction 2026/27 vs post-consultation expectations
findings.quote: The proposed funding formula published in June 2025 for consultation would have addressed the Council's repeated calls for fairer funding. Sadly, however, post consultation, the proposed formula was changed again to the significant detriment of the Council. For 2026/27, this led to a reduction of £14m compared with the funding levels previously modelled by the sector following the summer consultation, with the financial impact increasing significantly in subsequent years of the MTFP.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: The council's BEST transformation programme, which must deliver £28.6m of savings in 2027/28 and £30.2m in 2028/29, is currently at 'early stage' of detailed design with work due to accelerate mid-year.
findings.detail: Transformation savings are critical to closing the budget gap. The MTFP relies on £7.8m in 2026/27, £28.6m in 2027/28, and £30.2m in 2028/29 from the BEST transformation programme. However, the council admits 'detailed design work is at an early stage with initial workshops focussing on the transformation themes.' It forecasts 'fully aligned transformation delivery activity is expected to build through the year' from the second half 2026/27. The council explicitly warns: 'Failure to deliver at pace would increase financial risk and place additional pressure on in-year savings delivery and reserves.'
findings.matters: Nearly £30m of 2027/28 savings depend on a programme that has not yet moved beyond workshops. If transformation is delayed or delivers less than projected, the budget gap widens significantly.
findings.quote: The delivery of transformation savings is critical to the Council's financial sustainability over the MTFP period. These savings are profiled as follows £7.8m 2026/27, £28.6m 2027/28, £30.2m 2028/29... detailed design work is at an early stage with initial workshops focussing on the transformation themes being undertaken to identify and prioritise opportunities... There is therefore a direct and critical dependency between the successful delivery of this programme and the achievement of transformation savings. Failure to deliver at pace would increase financial risk and place additional pressure on in-year savings delivery and reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: The Financial Sustainability reserve is only £9.407m by end 2026/27 with a risk it will be drawn lower by emerging pressures, given £48.1m is locked into PFI risks.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes a £6.287m contribution to the Financial Sustainability reserve (with £5.3m transferred from another reserve), forecast to reach £9.407m by year-end. However, the council warns 'the risk of this being lower than currently forecast is significant' given 'significant pressures already emerging in 2026/27.' Separately, £48.1m is 'allocated to PFI risks' with 'a high likelihood that they will arise in a relatively short timeframe' (first hand-back March 2029).
findings.matters: A general resilience reserve of £9.4m is very thin for a council this size, especially when £48m is earmarked for specific PFI exit costs expected within three years.
findings.figures: £9.407m Financial Sustainability reserve by end 2026/27; £48.1m PFI risk reserve
findings.quote: The forecast balance of £9.407m by the end of the year is dependent upon whether the Council can deliver its services within the approved budget. Any overspend will be a first call on this reserve and, with significant pressures already emerging in 2026/27, the risk of this being lower than currently forecast is significant... c£48.1m is allocated to PFI risks. Although these costs may not crystallise immediately, the is a high likelihood that they will arise in a relatively short timeframe.

findings.headline: Reserves have declined by £232m (48%) in five years and are now below the average for comparator councils; the council needs £30m more to reach average coverage.
findings.detail: Council reserves fell from £484.347m (end 2020/21) to £252.865m (end 2025/26). At 24% of net revenue expenditure, they fall below the 28.4% average for comparator councils, requiring c£30m additional reserves to reach peer average. The forecast shows further decline to £224.509m by 2027/28. The council also notes that 'the rate at which reserves have reduced over the last 5 years is higher than the average' for comparators.
findings.matters: Declining reserves below comparator average signals eroding financial resilience. The council will have less buffer to absorb shocks or service pressures.
findings.figures: £484.347m (2020/21) to £252.865m (2025/26); 24% vs 28.4% average; need £30m more to reach average; forecast £224.509m by 2027/28
findings.quote: In previous years the Council's reserves have reduced significantly from £484.347m at the end 2020/21 to £252.865m at the end of 2025/26... Useable reserves for the Council, at the end of 2024/25, were below the average for comparator councils. In addition, the rate at which reserves have reduced over the last 5 years is higher than the average.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: Interest rates are forecast to be 0.5% higher than assumed in the current MTFP, and borrowing costs already consume 9% of net revenue budget — higher than comparator councils.
findings.detail: The council's treasury advisor MUFG has revised interest rate forecasts upward by 0.5% for 2026/27 and 2027/28 compared to the MTFP assumptions. Net interest payable is set at 9% of net revenue budget, which the council notes is 'higher than average percentage of the revenue budget supporting capital' when compared to other local authorities. This matters because the council has £1,054.80m of prudential borrowing across a £2,092.80m capital programme (50%), and borrowing costs are described as 'high compared to comparator authorities.'
findings.matters: Rising interest rates directly increase revenue costs that cannot be avoided. At 9% of revenue budget for borrowing, this is a substantial and growing commitment that crowds out service spending.
findings.figures: Interest rates 0.5% higher than forecast; net interest payable 9% of net revenue budget; £1,054.80m prudential borrowing of £2,092.80m capital programme
findings.quote: The Council's treasury advisor, MUFG, have updated their interest rate forecasting assumptions, since the version which was used in the Council's current MTFP. Interest rates are expected to be on average, 0.5% higher in 2026/27 and 2027/28 than was previously forecast... Borrowing costs for the Council are high compared to comparator authorities, and as at the 31 March 2026 the capital financing requirement (CFR, reflecting the underlying need to borrow) represented 55% of the Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) value on the balance sheet.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report

findings.headline: Pay inflation is now 3.3%-3.5%, higher than the 3% assumed in the budget, while non-pay inflation is forecast by the Bank of England at 3%-4% vs the 2% assumed in the MTFP.
findings.detail: The council's latest pay negotiations indicate a 3.3% award for 2026/27 (formal offer already rejected by unions), with worst-case assumption of 3.5%. The approved MTFP assumed 3%. For non-pay inflation, the BoE forecasts 3%-4% while the MTFP assumes 2%. The council has not yet reflected these higher inflation assumptions in the budget, treating them as a managed risk.
findings.matters: Inflation costs are recurring and large. A 0.3%-0.5% pay inflation variance across the council workforce is material; 1-2% non-pay inflation understatement compounds across contracts.
findings.figures: Pay: 3.3%-3.5% actual vs 3% assumed; Non-pay: 3%-4% BoE forecast vs 2% assumed
findings.quote: Latest negotiations for 2026/27, indicate that the actual increase will be higher than 3% due to the fact that a formal offer of 3.3% has already been rejected by the unions. The best-case now assumes a pay award of 3.3% and the worst-case 3.5%. Non-pay inflation has been assumed at an average of 2% in 2027/28 compared to the Bank of England forecast of 3%.

findings.headline: Collection Fund (council tax and business rates) is expected to generate £10.1m-£21.6m shortfalls in 2027/28, creating one-time funding pressures the council has not yet planned to manage.
findings.detail: Collection Fund forecasts show potential shortfalls ranging from £10.1m (best case) to £21.6m (worst case) in 2027/28. These are driven by collection rates, successful challenges through the Valuation Office Authority, and a review of single-persons discount. The council notes these figures are 'likely to change' and a 'planned review will inform a proposed approach on how the fluctuations in the collection fund can be managed and mitigated.' These are one-year pressures but material in size.
findings.matters: Collection Fund volatility is outside the council's direct control. Shortfalls of £10-21m will either force service cuts or reserve draws in a single year.
findings.figures: £10.1m-£21.6m shortfall in 2027/28; best case £0.5m cumulative 2027/28-2028/29; worst case £8m cumulative
findings.quote: Collection Fund related pressures are forecast to create a gap ranging from £0.5m to £8m over the two financial years, however there are some significant shortfalls (ranging from £10.1m - £21.6m) that will need to be managed in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: The High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant has a cumulative deficit of £137.148m by end 2026/27, with future grant funding subject to Department for Education approval and uncertain beyond 2025/26.
findings.detail: SEND/High Needs spending far exceeds the dedicated grant. The council forecasts an in-year deficit of £55.996m in 2026/27 and a cumulative deficit of £137.148m before potential High Needs Stability Grant. Demand for Education, Health and Care Plans is forecast to grow 20% in the next 12 months, with overall EHCP numbers projected to rise 9% by 2029. The council is investing in local capacity but relies on future grant funding that 'remains subject to Department for Education approval' and has 'uncertainty around the future treatment of DSG deficits beyond 2025/26.'
findings.matters: A £137m cumulative deficit is a material liability. If the DfE does not cover it as expected, it becomes a council budget problem. The 20% growth in SEND demand is uncontrollable and will drive costs higher.
findings.figures: £55.996m in-year 2026/27; £137.148m cumulative by end 2026/27; 20% demand growth forecast next 12 months
findings.quote: Significant financial pressures persist within the High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) budget, driven by continued growth in demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and a funding position that remains effectively cash-flat in 2026/27. Demand is forecast to increase by 20% over the next 12 months... the High Needs budget has been updated through the local SEND reform plan, with an in-year deficit of £55.996m, contributing to a forecast 2026/27 cumulative deficit of £137.148m, before the potential impact of the High Needs Stability Grant, which remains subject to Department for Education (DfE) approval.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: A £5m restructuring/people savings target is already at risk, forcing the council to create a recruitment panel to find alternative one-off savings.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget included £5m of savings to be achieved through restructuring aligned to the council's People Strategy. The council now states this saving 'is at risk' and has established a recruitment panel to identify one-off savings to mitigate the pressure in-year. This is happening while the council is undertaking LGA-supported organizational redesign work (spans and layers review) which is only in 'discovery phase' due to complete in October 2026.
findings.matters: A high-value savings programme that is already at risk in year one signals either poor planning or external factors preventing delivery. This reduces the credibility of future savings targets.
findings.figures: £5m at-risk savings
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget includes a savings target of £5m that was to be achieved through ensuring that we have the right management and decision-making structures in place in line with our People Strategy objective to right-size the organisation. The achievement of this saving is at risk, and a recruitment panel has been created to identify one off savings, to mitigate this pressure in year.

findings.headline: Only 78% of the 2025/26 savings target was achieved, and the council expects some of this non-delivery to recur into 2027/28.
findings.detail: In 2025/26, the council delivered £38.112m of a £48.825m savings target. The shortfall was £10.713m (22%). The council explicitly notes that 'some of this non-delivery will be recurring,' meaning the structural gap in savings delivery will persist. This comes as the council relies on £59.113m of new savings in 2026/27 and £48.842m in 2027/28.
findings.matters: If the council cannot reliably deliver planned savings, the budget gap will be larger than modelled. A lender needs to know whether the council's savings plans are achievable or optimistic.
findings.figures: £38.112m achieved of £48.825m target (78%); £10.713m shortfall
findings.quote: In 2025/26, £38.112m (78%) of the approved £48.825m savings target was achieved. As some of this non-delivery will be recurring, an assessment of the deliverability of these, including through transformation activity, will be carried out over the summer.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: The council forecasts a budget gap of £22m in 2027/28 alone (best case), or up to £20.9m across two years, with no agreed mitigation strategy yet in place.
findings.detail: Three scenarios model service and funding pressures separately. The best case shows £11.9m service pressures in 2027/28 and £10.1m Collection Fund shortfalls, totalling £22m. The mid-range and worst-case scenarios are significantly higher, ranging to £20.9m cumulative. The council has asked directorates to identify options totalling 5% of expenditure but has not yet determined how the full gap will be closed.
findings.matters: A £22m gap in one year (2% of net revenue budget) is substantial and means the council will need to cut services, raise income, or draw reserves significantly. The council admits 'there will be a gap for the Council to address - even in the best-case scenario.'
findings.quote: The scenarios combined, summarised in the two tables below, indicate a potential total budget gap of between £10.3m and £20.9m over the next two financial years with the best-case scenario forecasting a gap of £22m in 2027/28 – approximately 2% of the net revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Report
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199470/199470.pdf
findings.headline: The council drew £7.494m from reserves in 2025/26 to close an overspend, indicating an underlying structural imbalance in budget that the s151 officer describes as unsustainable.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 outturn had sustained demand-led pressures in children's and adult social care, plus exceptional severe weather costs. Although mitigation actions reduced the overall overspend, the council had to use reserve funding to balance the position. The s151 officer flags this as 'potentially highlighting an underlying structural imbalance between demand and available resources.'
findings.matters: Using reserves to close in-year gaps is a sign of structural problems in the budget that will persist. A lender needs to know if the council can operate within its means.
findings.figures: £7.494m overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: Although in-year mitigation actions reduced the overall overspend, the use of reserve funding to close the final overspend of £7.494m was required, potentially highlighting an underlying structural imbalance between demand and available resources. This is not sustainable and leaves the Council exposed to ongoing financial risk that needs to be addressed in the MTFP.

findings.headline: Transformation success is explicitly measured against the requirement not to draw on reserves.
findings.detail: The document states that by March 2029, success means "transformation savings have landed in budgets" and "The £154.101m of MTFP savings has been delivered without unplanned recourse to reserves". This framing reveals that reserves drawdown is the fallback if savings slip.
findings.matters: Councils with high reliance on reserves to bridge budget gaps have reduced financial flexibility and higher risk. The explicit measurement against reserve usage signals this is a real concern for the council's finance team.
findings.figures: £154.101m savings target; implies reserves are available to cover shortfalls if savings do not materialise
findings.quote: The £154.101m of MTFP savings has been delivered without unplanned recourse to reserves and without cutting the services residents value most.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Appendix 1
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199471/199471.pdf
findings.headline: External peer review identified risks of double-counting savings between different savings lines, requiring new governance controls.
findings.detail: The LGA Corporate Peer Challenge flagged this as a material risk. The new BEST framework is explicitly designed to "prevent double counting" of savings across transformation, demand management, commissioning and service efficiency categories. This suggests the council has previously (or nearly) counted the same saving twice across different lines.
findings.matters: Double-counting would mask a real deficit. If savings are being counted multiple times across lines, the true financial position is worse than reported. The need for new controls to prevent this indicates it has been an identified weakness.
findings.figures: No figures on extent of double-counting risk
findings.quote: The LGA Corporate Peer Challenge and other external insight reinforced the need for prioritisation, strong governance and controls that prevent double counting.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Appendix 1
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199471/199471.pdf
findings.headline: Significant structural demand pressures in Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, SEND and Housing are driving the need for transformation.
findings.detail: These are the council's highest-cost and fastest-growing service areas. The document identifies ongoing demand pressures as a core driver of the transformation need, suggesting these are structural (not cyclical) and will persist. The framework includes a specific Prevention & Integrated Care transformation theme aimed at managing these pressures.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils partly on the trajectory of their highest-cost services. Persistent demand pressure in social care and housing, combined with inflation in the cost base, creates a structural deficit that must be managed by efficiency or service redesign rather than demand reduction alone.
findings.figures: No specific demand growth figures provided in this document
findings.quote: Demand pressures remain significant in Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, SEND and Housing. Inflation and contractual cost pressures have changed the cost base of key services.

findings.paper_title: 2027/28 Budget and MTFP Refresh - Strategic Framework, Transformation approach and Emerging Issues - Appendix 1
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s199471/199471.pdf
findings.headline: The council's financial plan depends entirely on delivering £154.1m in savings, with 43% dependent on transformation success.
findings.detail: The MTFP is balanced only through committed savings delivery across multiple categories. The BEST Transformation Programme is the single largest source, targeting £66.672m over three years. No alternative funding plan is mentioned. Success is explicitly framed as achieving savings "without unplanned recourse to reserves", implying reserves would be drawn if savings do not materialise.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can balance its budget without drawing reserves. If the £66.7m transformation savings do not land as planned, the council has no disclosed plan B.
findings.figures: Total MTFP savings £154.101m; Transformation Programme £66.672m (43.3% of total); Transformation investment £19.5m; Savings as percentage of net revenue budget: 6.6% (2026/27), 5.2% (2027/28), 4.7% (2028/29)
findings.quote: The MTFP is balanced, but that balance depends on sustained delivery of savings and efficiencies, including transformation, demand management, commissioning reform and service efficiency.

findings.detail: The council had to use reserves to close the final overspend in 2025/26 because in-year mitigation actions were insufficient. findings.headline: The council has established new governance and controls following external advice about risks of double-counting and inconsistent discipline.
findings.detail: The Framework responds to findings from the LGA Corporate Peer Challenge which 'reinforced the need for prioritisation, strong governance and controls that prevent double counting.' The new BEST Framework introduces mandatory business case discipline, a Design Finance and Assurance Authority gate, and single version of truth reporting to prevent savings being claimed multiple times across different workstreams.
findings.matters: The emphasis on anti-double-counting controls suggests historical control weaknesses or peer challenge findings about savings discipline. Tighter controls indicate the council recognizes this as a risk area.
findings.figures: £154.101m savings target; 43.3% from transformation; £19.5m transformation investment
findings.quote: The LGA Corporate Peer Challenge and other external insight reinforced the need for prioritisation, strong governance and controls that prevent double counting.

findings.headline: Transformation savings represent 43.3% of the total savings requirement, creating concentration risk in a change programme.
findings.detail: Of £154.101m total savings, £66.672m (43.3%) is expected to come from transformation programmes. The council is committing £19.5m of transformation investment over three years to deliver this, and the document notes this investment is 'modest compared with the total savings requirement.' Transformation depends on sustained delivery of redesign initiatives across multiple services.
findings.matters: Transformation savings carry higher delivery risk than operational efficiency. Concentration of 43% of savings in transformation programmes means service redesign failures would materially impact the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £66.672m transformation savings (43.3% of total), £19.5m transformation investment over three years, representing 13% of transformation savings requirement
findings.quote: Because the investment is modest compared with the total savings requirement, it must be directed to the work with the strongest evidence, greatest strategic fit and clearest delivery route.

findings.headline: The council's balanced budget depends on delivery of £154.101m of savings over three years in an environment of significant demand pressures.
findings.detail: The MTFP is stated to be balanced, but explicitly depends on delivering sustained savings and efficiencies. Demand pressures are significant in Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, SEND and Housing. The council faces £59.113m of required savings in 2026/27 alone (6.6% of net revenue budget), rising to cumulative target of £154.101m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the structural risk: if demand grows faster than anticipated or savings plans fail to land, the budget will move into deficit with no identified buffer.
findings.figures: £154.101m total savings required over three years; £59.113m (2026/27), £48.842m (2027/28), £46.146m (2028/29); savings as percentage of net revenue budget: 6.6% (2026/27), 5.2% (2027/28), 4.7% (2028/29)
findings.quote: The MTFP is balanced, but that balance depends on sustained delivery of savings and efficiencies, including transformation, demand management, commissioning reform and service efficiency.

findings.headline: CIFCA generated a surplus of £226,889 in 2025/26 and increased reserves by 26%, demonstrating financial resilience despite operational challenges from staff absence.
findings.detail: Despite the staffing disruption and its impact on operational processes, CIFCA's activities across departments produced a significant surplus that was added to reserves. Total reserves increased from £859,330 to £1,086,219, representing a 26% increase. Auditors confirmed that year-end financial records have been fully reconciled and accounts accurately represent CIFCA's financial position. This demonstrates that underlying financial management remained sound even during the period when governance procedures were being worked around.
findings.matters: Growing reserves provide financial flexibility to absorb shocks and fund future priorities, signalling to a lender that the authority can weather operational disruptions and to a finance director that capacity exists for planned investments.
findings.figures: Surplus of £226,889; reserves increased from £859,330 to £1,086,219

findings.headline: A key staff member's prolonged absence exposed gaps in standard operating procedures, creating operational challenges including delays in fuel card processing and difficulties with petty cash administration.
findings.detail: A key staff member's sudden prolonged absence required significant changes to established financial processes. While core financial controls remained effective with high-value payments properly authorized, operational challenges emerged including delays in fuel card processing and gaps in documented petty cash procedures. The audit identifies a Medium priority finding: without comprehensive standard operating procedures and cross-training, there is a 'heightened possibility of inconsistent practices, inefficient claim processing, and challenges in maintaining adequate segregation of duties' during future staff absences.
findings.matters: Organizational resilience and key-person dependency risk the continuity of financial controls and compliance during staffing changes, affecting both a lender's confidence in control environment stability and a finance director's ability to maintain internal controls.

findings.quote: delays in fuel card processing were noted, and the reassignment of petty cash responsibilities highlighted gaps in documented procedures, with difficulties encountered in claim submission, VAT coding, and accessing timely guidance, indicating a need for clearer standard operating procedures

findings.detail: The team carrying out the annual assurance opinion on governance, risk and control is operating below the staffing levels of comparable councils. Under-resourcing of audit weakens the Council's ability to identify and escalate emerging problems.
findings.matters: The assurance opinion (reasonable assurance) that underpins governance confidence is only as good as the audit team that generates it. A lean audit function may miss emerging risks or be unable to follow up on findings with sufficient depth.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s197154/Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Appendix 1.pdf
findings.headline: Limited Assurance on officers' declarations of interest, gifts and hospitality — policy outdated and controls weak
findings.detail: Internal audit found the declarations policy (last reviewed 2017) is inconsistently applied, automation attempts failed, manual processes are poorly monitored, and compliance rates are low. Management oversight is weak with little counter-signatory review. Declaration forms lack critical elements such as secondary employment provisions.
findings.matters: Weak controls over conflicts of interest is a governance red flag. If the Council cannot reliably know what outside interests its officers hold, transparency and decision quality are at risk; lenders rely on governance strength as a proxy for competent management.
findings.figures: Policy last reviewed 2017; automation attempts unsuccessful; compliance rates low
findings.quote: The policy, last reviewed in 2017, is outdated, referencing obsolete systems and failing to reflect current practices or alternative solutions. The outdated policy is inconsistently applied across services and attempts to implement a centralised compliance tool have so far been unsuccessful, resulting in manual processes that are poorly monitored and unreliable.

findings.headline: High risk that required savings will not be delivered in future MTFP years, with difficulty accelerating
findings.detail: Internal audit has flagged a high-risk finding that the difficulty of achieving savings increases year-on-year, because the easier, more efficient savings are being exhausted first. This means years 2 and 3 of the MTFP face escalating delivery risk.
findings.matters: If year one already requires a £9.1m reserve draw despite having the easier savings still available, years two and three face materially higher risk. A lender funding a council that cannot balance its budget without reserve depletion is taking on a credit deterioration path.
findings.figures: £160m three-year savings target; £9.1m drawn in year 1
findings.quote: Each successive year the risks of not being able to deliver the savings will increase as the savings that could more efficiently be delivered have already been achieved.

findings.headline: £9.1m drawn from Financial Sustainability Reserve in 2025-26 due to unmet savings targets
findings.detail: The Council failed to deliver the cost pressures and savings required to balance the 2025-26 budget, requiring a £9.1m drawdown from reserves. This is part of a three-year MTFP with a £160m total savings target. The reserve depletion signals that budget management is running behind plan.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the Council can actually deliver the savings it plans on; a £9.1m shortfall in year one signals either over-optimism in forecasting or weakening delivery capability.
findings.figures: £9.1m drawdown from Financial Sustainability Reserve; £160m three-year savings target
findings.quote: The cost pressures and savings required to balance the budget in 2025/26 have not been delivered in full, requiring £9.1m to be drawn down from the Financial Sustainability Reserve.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s197120/Chief Internal Auditor Annual Report 2025-26 - Appendix 1.pdf
findings.headline: Delay in social care system migration threatens cost control and demand management for high-budget directorate
findings.detail: Migration of the Mosaic case management system to cloud has been delayed, pushing completion of planned efficiency improvements to post-April 2026. This delays integration of key procurement and commissioning systems needed to manage rapidly increasing demand for direct payments. The review flagged high residual risk that cost control and service delivery objectives of the Direct Payment First initiative may not be achieved.
findings.matters: Delays to system infrastructure and process improvements create risk that a high-budget, growing directorate cannot manage cost escalation; particular concern given Together for Families budget pressures are already acknowledged as significant.
findings.figures: Delays push system deliverables to post-April 2026; high residual risk rating
findings.quote: The review concluded that the residual risk was however high due to the delay in implementation of planned efficiency measures such as the Virtual Wallet system affecting the ability of the service to meet the forecasted increase in demand for DPs. Without the deployment of those planned efficiencies, the significant risk of non-achievement of the objectives of the Direct Payment First initiative, namely, cost control and improved service delivery, was flagged in the report.

findings.headline: Contract management controls are inconsistent and create governance and statutory compliance risk
findings.detail: Auditors gave Limited Assurance on Contract Management across strategic and critical contracts. Compliance with approved procedures is 'partial and inconsistent', exposing the council to governance, statutory compliance (Procurement Act 2023), and value-for-money risks on its most important supplier relationships.
findings.matters: Weak contract management controls on strategic contracts undermine cost control, value-for-money assurance, and statutory compliance; creates contingent liability and supplier relationship risk.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion on Contract Management
findings.quote: In respect of Contract Management, we gave a Limited Assurance opinion - while examples of good contract management practice were observed, compliance with the current approved version of the Contract Management Operating Model, Toolkit and associated procedures is partial and inconsistent. As a result, the Council remains exposed to governance, statutory compliance (with the Procurement Act 2023), and value for money risks in relation to its strategic and critical contracts.

findings.headline: Material reduction in forecast capital spend; MTFP capital spending cut from £377m to £260m year-on-year

findings.headline: Savings plan at high risk of failure, requiring drawdown from reserves to balance 2025-26 budget
findings.detail: Auditors flagged significant risk that required savings in excess of £150m will not be delivered in each of the three years of the Medium Term Financial Plan. The cost pressures and savings needed to balance 2025-26 were not delivered in full, forcing the council to withdraw £9.1m from its Financial Sustainability Reserve. Auditors note that each successive year will see higher risks of non-delivery as the easier savings have been exhausted.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to balance operating budgets signals deteriorating financial flexibility and sustainability; failure to deliver savings in the medium term is a material financial stability concern for lenders.
findings.figures: £9.1m drawn from Financial Sustainability Reserve; savings target in excess of £150m over three-year MTFP
findings.quote: Although providing reasonable assurance, the audit of Financial Reporting and Savings Monitoring highlighted there is a high risk that the required savings (in excess of £150m) will not be delivered in each of the three years of the Medium Term Financial Plan. The cost pressures and savings required to balance the budget in 2025/26 have not been delivered in full, requiring £9.1m to be drawn down from the Financial Sustainability Reserve.

findings.headline: Capital programme financing shifted to rely £30.4m more on borrowing after grant funding fell £13.1m and capital receipts fell £18.0m, increasing future debt-servicing costs.
findings.detail: The revised 2025/26 capital forecast (£373.6m) fundamentally changed financing mix: grant funding forecast to drop £13.1m, capital receipts fall £18.0m, but Council increased borrowing by £30.4m to maintain fully funded programme. The report explicitly warns this "will impact the CFR in future years, directly increasing the pressure on debt-servicing costs in revenue." This impact has been factored into 2026/27 budget and future Capital and Investment Strategy.
findings.matters: Shifting from grants and receipts to borrowing increases leverage and future revenue expenditure on debt service. If capital schemes slip or fail to generate expected receipts, debt-servicing pressure will intensify rapidly.
findings.figures: Grant funding down £13.1m; capital receipts down £18.0m; borrowing increased £30.4m; CFR forecast £48.4m (£3m below budget)

Grant funding is forecast to drop by £13.1m and capital receipts fall by £18.0m, due largely to project rephasing and a reprioritisation of capital receipt allocation. To maintain a fully funded programme, the Council has increased borrowing £30.4m.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will reach £80.6m by 31 March 2026 and is projected to spiral to c£180m when statutory override ends in March 2028.
findings.detail: The council set a deficit budget of £27m for DSG in 2025/26, but Q3 forecast outturn is £35.2m, increasing cumulative deficit to £80.6m. When the statutory override expires in March 2028, the deficit is forecast to rise to c£180m. The deficit is driven by EHCP demand growth: children with EHCPs expected to grow 13% this year to 5,859 and a further 15% in 2026/27. DSG costs increased £8.2m, driven by living wage uplift to top-up rates and Post 16 increases.
findings.matters: A £180m cumulative DSG deficit is a critical structural problem. The statutory override mechanism is temporary; the council faces escalating revenue pressure when this ends unless government reforms DSG funding or the council finds substantial recurring cost reductions.
findings.figures: Q3 forecast outturn £35.2m (vs £27m budget); cumulative deficit £80.6m at 31 March 2026; projected c£180m when override ends March 2028; EHCP growth 13% this year (to 5,859), further 15% forecast 2026/27
findings.quote: A £27m deficit budget was set for 2025/26 for the ring-fenced Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG). The quarter 3 forecast outturn of £35.2m increases the cumulative reserve deficit to £80.6m at 31 March 2026. Based on current forecasts, the deficit will rise to c£180m when the statutory override ends in March 2028.

findings.headline: Savings target is severely underperfoming: only 69% delivered by Q3 with £7.8m to deliver in final quarter, and most mitigations are one-off and do not address underlying pressures.
findings.detail: Council set a £48.8m savings target for 2025/26 but forecasts delivery of only £39.1m (80%) by year-end, a shortfall of £9.7m. Even after identifying £6.5m of mitigations, the net budget impact remains £3.2m. By Q3 only £31.3m had been delivered (69%), leaving £7.8m to deliver in the final quarter. Children's services undelivered savings of £3.2m (house fostering capacity, in-house homes opening delayed) and Adult Services unable to fully deliver MTFP savings. The report explicitly states most corporate savings are one-off and "do not address the underlying pressures."
findings.matters: Recurring structural overspends in Adult Care and Children's services are being masked by one-off corporate savings and reserve drawdowns, indicating the council cannot sustainably balance its budget without fundamental service change.
findings.figures: £48.8m target, £39.1m forecast (80%); £3.2m net shortfall after mitigations; £31.3m delivered by Q3 (69%); £7.8m to deliver in Q4
findings.quote: Without these mitigations the overspend would have been significantly higher. However, most of these savings are one off and do not address the underlying pressures within the two directorates that continue to face significant overspends.

findings.headline: Children in care placement costs rising structurally, with independent children's homes up to 73 places (from 55 at year start) and court-ordered parent-child assessments up to 11 (from 2).
findings.detail: Children in care numbers rose to 654 (up 18 from Q2, 16 from year-end 2024/25). Independent children's homes places jumped from 55 at start of year to 73 by Q3. Court-ordered parent-child residential assessments rocketed from 2 at year start to 11 by Q3, adding £0.5m to forecast since Q2. findings.detail: The council is deliberately maintaining 38-39% of borrowing in short-term instruments (due under 12 months or LOBO call dates) rather than locking into long-term fixed rates. findings.matters: This is not a cyclical pressure that will improve; it is a structural deterioration in Cornwall's relative funding allocation. findings.headline: The council's Section 151 Officer explicitly considered issuing a Section 114 notice (insolvency marker) and assessed the risk as 'low' but not zero
findings.detail: The narrative report contains a section titled 'Consideration of the Issuing of a Section 114 Notice', explaining what triggers one and the constraints it places on the council. The S151 Officer then states 'the likelihood of it needing to issue a S114 notice in the short to medium term as "low"'. This language—explicitly considering it, then rating risk as low rather than negligible—indicates material concern about balanced budget risk in the medium term (typically 3-5 years).
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is issued when a council expects its spending to exceed income (violating Local Government Finance Act 1988). It is a statutory insolvency trigger. The fact that it was considered signals the council's own finance officer saw material risk of this outcome. Even a 'low' assessment suggests 20-30% subjective probability, not negligible.
findings.figures: None (narrative statement only)
findings.quote: A S114 notice is a serious undertaking and places restrictions on what the Authority can do and the actions it must take. Cornwall Council has well-established financial planning processes... The Council considers that the likelihood of it needing to issue a S114 notice in the short to medium term as "low".

findings.headline: Usable reserves fell by £82.3m in one year to £250m, as the council deployed reserves to avoid budget deficit
findings.detail: Total usable reserves declined from £332.348m to £250.046m, a decline of 24.7% in a single year. This is not due to accounting adjustments—the Movement in Reserves Statement shows a net cash outflow of £82.3m. The council explicitly states in its narrative that it is 'deploying a prudent level of reserves' to manage budget pressures and ensure 'its budget incorporates demand-led growth'. This is reserve depletion to cover operating costs, not capital investment.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate is unsustainable. At the current trajectory, the council would exhaust general reserves in under 20 years; accelerated by demand pressure, far sooner. Lenders rely on reserves as a buffer. A £82m outflow in one year signals the council cannot balance the budget on operations alone.
findings.figures: Usable reserves fell from £332.348m (31 March 2024) to £250.046m (31 March 2025), a decrease of £82.302m; General Fund alone down £2.416m
findings.quote: The Council is expending every financial sinew it can muster attempting to balance the books, including deploying a prudent level of reserves, to ensure that its budget incorporates demand-led growth

The combination of rising short-term borrowing, falling investments, and overdraft position is a stress signal.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Statement of Accounts and Audit Findings Report for Cornwall Council - Appendix 2 , item A/170
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cornwall.gov.uk/documents/s193641/202425 Statement of Accounts and Audit Findings Report for Cornwall Council - Appendix 2.pdf
findings.headline: Journal approval control failures: two unapproved journals posted and routine year-end journals approved in advance without amount verification.
findings.detail: Testing identified two instances of journals not being approved per the Council's approval procedure. Additionally, the auditor noted that some routine year-end journals are approved in advance (e.g., depreciation charge approvals given before the amount is known), which defeats the control purpose of confirming both appropriateness AND correctness of the amount. This weakness was also raised in the prior year and remains unaddressed.
findings.matters: Journal approval is a fundamental fraud control; unapproved journals and advance approvals without amount verification create a window for unauthorized or erroneous postings and suggest management override risk is not being effectively mitigated.
findings.figures: Two instances of unapproved journals
findings.quote: Our testing identified two instances of journals not being approved. Officers should be reminded of the Council's journal approval procedure in order to ensure the Council's processes are followed. Routine checks should be introduced to ensure this is the case. We also noted that some of the routine year-end journals are approved in advance (e.g. permission is given to post the journals relating to the depreciation charge for the year). Whilst we recognise the time pressures associated with the close-down process, the approvals process fulfils two purposes: agreement that the journal is appropriate; and confirmation that the amount is correct. When journals are approved in advance, the check on the amounts involved is missed and hence the control is not as effective as the Council intended.

Despite a year of work, key elements remain outstanding or not fully embedded: the S117 aftercare procedure under the Mental Health Act is still being developed and not yet implemented. This is a statutory governance failure.
findings.matters: Incomplete joint governance arrangements create legal liability and risk service failures in care provision. This could result in complaints to the ombudsman, litigation, or care safeguarding incidents.
findings.figures: Issue ongoing since 2023/24; internal audit rescheduled to first half of 2025/26
findings.quote: Despite some progress in the joint governance arrangements with the NHS there is still some areas of work which are outstanding or not yet embedded... The Standard operating procedure for S117 aftercare under the Mental Health Act is still being developed and this needs to be finalised, adopted and implemented.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024 25 - Appendix 1
findings.paper_url: harness:2026-01-13:Annual Governance Statement 2024 25 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Accruals controls are weak and there is a risk that accruals artificially inflate budgets
findings.detail: Internal audit identified that there is no formalised review process for accruals (creditors/payables). This creates a risk that budgets are being inflated by unrealistic accrual estimates, or that accruals are being raised without proper supporting evidence or approval. This is a material control weakness in financial reporting.
findings.matters: Weak accruals controls can hide the true financial position. Accruals that are overstated can mask deficits. This is particularly concerning given the DSG deficit issue.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: The review of accruals raised concerns about the risk of raised accruals artificially inflating budgets due to the lack of a formalised review process. There is also a risk for accruals to be raised with insufficient supporting evidence or approval.

findings.headline: Internal Audit is significantly under-resourced and cannot provide full coverage of governance risks
findings.detail: The Council's internal audit team is substantially under-staffed compared to similar authorities. This limits the Council's ability to audit its own operations and identify control weaknesses early. The team is unable to provide comprehensive assurance over governance and financial controls.
findings.matters: Under-resourced internal audit means the Council cannot identify emerging financial or governance problems. It weakens the control environment at a time when the Council faces structural budget pressures.
findings.figures: Team 'significantly under-resourced compared with other similar authorities'
findings.quote: The overall performance and output of the Internal Audit service need to be considered against the backdrop of its current resource levels. The team is significantly under-resourced compared with other similar authorities.

findings.detail: In the interim Auditor's Annual Report for 2024/25 issued in November 2025, the external auditor formally identified one significant weakness in the Council's financial arrangements. This is an audit finding that must be reported and remediated. It relates specifically to how the Council is managing the DSG structural deficit and the governance arrangements for SEND transformation.
findings.matters: A 'significant weakness' rating in external audit on financial sustainability is a red flag for lenders. It indicates the external auditor does not have full confidence in the Council's ability to manage its finances through the medium term.
findings.figures: One significant weakness identified in Financial Sustainability arrangements
findings.quote: The auditors identified one significant weakness in the Council's Financial Sustainability arrangements in respect of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2024 25 - Appendix 1
findings.paper_url: harness:2026-01-13:Annual Governance Statement 2024 25 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: DSG deficit could threaten the Council's solvency if the statutory override ends in 2028
findings.detail: The Council faces a structural funding problem in the Dedicated Schools Grant (SEND services) with rising demand but a cash-flat budget. The government's statutory override, which allows councils to spread DSG deficits over multiple years, is due to end on 31 March 2028. The Council has implemented a fortnightly DSG working group to manage spending, but has no clear plan for how to address existing deficits, and is awaiting government clarification on how the transition will be managed.
findings.matters: This is an existential solvency risk. Unlike most budget pressures, DSG is a statutory service the Council must deliver. If deficits cannot be managed within the override period, the Council's reserves could be wiped out.
findings.figures: 2025-26 budget is 'cash flat'; DSG override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Additionally, the potential removal of the DSG statutory override in 2028 could threaten the Council's solvency... In advance of the government reforming the system, the Council needs to set out how it intends to reduce spend alongside the continued increased demand. This work is currently in progress.

findings.headline: HRA recharge to General Fund lacks supporting evidence and relies on historic data; Council now reviewing
findings.detail: A £1.279m journal reallocating Council support costs to the Housing Revenue Account had limited supporting evidence, with most costs based on historic information rather than current allocations. The HRA is statutory and ringfenced; recharging from the General Fund requires clear allocation. The Council is undertaking a review of this recharge process for 2025/26.
findings.matters: The HRA must be kept separately with its own income, expenditure and reserves. Unjustified recharges can distort both accounts and create cross-subsidy risk. The fact that the auditor flagged lack of supporting evidence and the Council is only now reviewing suggests control has been lax.

findings.paper_url: harness:2026-01-13:202425 Statement of Accounts and Audit Findings Report for Cornwall Council - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Journal approval controls broken: two unapproved journals found and year-end journals pre-approved without amount verification
findings.detail: Testing found two instances of journals not being approved. Additionally, routine year-end journals are approved in advance (e.g., depreciation journals) without checking amounts are correct, meaning the approval is checking appropriateness but not correctness. Officers should be reminded of the Council's journal approval procedure. This was raised in 2023/24 but not fixed.
findings.matters: Journal controls are a core internal control to prevent error and fraud. If journals are not being approved or are pre-approved without checking amounts, the Council lacks a basic safeguard. This directly undermines the reliability of the financial statements.
findings.figures: Two unapproved journals identified; year-end journals pre-approved
findings.quote: Our testing identified two instances of journals not being approved. Officers should be reminded of the Council's journal approval procedure in order to ensure the Council's processes are followed. Routine checks should be introduced to ensure this is the case.

findings.headline: Council dwellings valuation overstated by £12m due to asset transfer and duplication errors
findings.detail: Testing of council dwelling valuations identified an error of approximately £12m. One project was included twice; two other projects transferred from assets under construction were aggregated instead of being recorded at individual asset level. The Council has corrected the errors: Revaluation Reserve overstated by £9.844m and impairment overstated by £2.016m.
findings.matters: A £12m error in the largest single asset class (£562m council dwellings at 31 March 2025) shows gaps in asset controls. Although corrected, it raises questions about the robustness of fixed asset accounting and the council's ability to track and value its property portfolio.
findings.figures: Error approximately £12m; council dwellings valued at £562m; Revaluation Reserve overstated by £9.844m; impairment overstated by £2.016m
findings.quote: We have identified an error of approximately £12m, from our Council Dwellings valuations review, related to the transfer of assets from assets under construction to operational assets. Our testing found that one project had been included twice, which resulted in the council dwelling values being overstated.

findings.matters: DSG is a ringfenced grant for schools spending; weakness here suggests either schools are overspending their budgets without proper Council oversight, or the Council cannot control spending it is legally responsible for. findings.headline: Unitary council governance is now minority administration following May 2025 elections
findings.detail: Following council elections in May 2025, no single party gained overall control. A coalition of Liberal Democrats and Independents formed a minority administration. This creates risk that the administration cannot command majority support on budget decisions or service changes.
findings.matters: Minority administrations in financial stress often face difficulty making hard decisions (cuts, service reductions) when they lack majority backing. Budget setting and savings delivery become politically fragile.

findings.quote: Cornwall Council elections were held in May 2025 with no single party gaining overall control. This is not uncommon in Cornwall and a coalition of parties was formed by Liberal Democrats and Independents forming a minority administration to run the Council.

findings.detail: Cash and cash equivalents moved from a positive £46.646m to a negative (overdrawn) £4.451m. This £51m swing in cash position suggests the council is drawing on overdraft facilities to meet day-to-day obligations, a sign of cash flow stress.
findings.matters: A council in overdraft is funding operations from short-term debt rather than from reserves or cash generation. This is unsustainable and signals immediate pressure on liquidity.

findings.headline: Usable reserves fallen by £82m in one year to £250m, now being depleted faster than forecast
findings.detail: The council's total usable reserves fell from £332.348m at 31 March 2024 to £250.046m at 31 March 2025. This £82.3m reduction is being used to balance the budget. The general fund reserve specifically fell from £41.184m to £38.768m.
findings.matters: A council deploying reserves at this rate will exhaust them within 3 years if the trend continues. Reserves are the lender's backstop for service continuity. Watching their depletion is watching runway consumption.

findings.matters: An overspend after savings attempts shows the council is struggling to contain service demand and costs. Combined with failed CFS savings, this suggests a systematic problem with budget delivery.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £45.4m with no resolution beyond 2028
findings.detail: The council carries an unusable DSG reserve of £45.372m, an increase of £22.442m in one year. The deficit is driven by demand for special educational needs provision. A statutory override protecting the council from having to balance this against the general fund is in place only until 31 March 2028, leaving three years to solve a structural problem.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a statutory protection is about to expire on a growing liability. The council has no articulated plan for managing this deficit when the override ends, and demand-driven growth in SEND is a nationwide trend with no obvious solution.
findings.figures: £45.372m reserve, £22.442m increase in one year, override expires 2028
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25, the Council had an unusable reserve relating to Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) amounting to £45.372m, an increase of £22.442m, this relates to a statutory override in place till 31st March 2028. The purpose of this reserve is to fund the deficits within the DSG budgets, these costs are driven by increased demand for special educational needs and disabilities.

findings.headline: If the tag fee is not increased or tolls not revised, both parent authorities will face mandatory revenue funding calls to cover operating deficits starting in 2029/30.

findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council has hidden liabilities or is exposed to funding calls from joint ventures. Here, both councils face a known, dated obligation to fund a deteriorating toll service if it cannot self-sustain—a claim that will crystallise unless fees are raised or tolls revised.

findings.headline: Virgin Media court ruling creates unquantified contingent liability for historical pension scheme amendments made 1996-2016
findings.detail: The UK High Court ruled in June 2023 (affirmed July 2024) that certain amendments to contracted-out pension schemes may be invalid if not supported by actuarial certificates under section 37 of the Pension Schemes Act 1993. The government actuary is reviewing whether certificates exist for all relevant amendments, but the assessment remains incomplete as at the date of the accounts.
findings.matters: This is an unquantified tail risk: if historical amendments are found invalid, the fund's liabilities could materially increase with no reserve held to cover the cost. A lender needs visibility of potential hidden obligations.

findings.headline: Council deliberately holds 52% of borrowing short-term, betting on interest rates falling before refinancing
findings.detail: The council has £738.8m of its £1,422.1m borrowing (52%) in loans under 12 months maturity. Long-term borrowing rates remain elevated and the council is avoiding locking in higher costs, intending instead to refinance into longer-term borrowing once rates fall. No long-term borrowing has been taken out in 2025/26 to date.
findings.matters: This is a rate-timing bet. If interest rates remain elevated or rise further, refinancing costs spike when short-term loans mature, pressuring debt servicing budgets and council cash flow.
findings.figures: £738.8m short-term borrowing (52% of total), zero long-term borrowing in 2025/26 to date
findings.quote: The cost of long-term borrowing is still elevated due to inflation concerns and new concerns around the economic impact of potential announcements in the Autumn Budget, meaning the Council continues to use a strategy of taking out short-term borrowing to keep costs lower, until longer-term rates reduce, at which point the Council can lock in at a lower cost, for longer-term certainty of cost.
